title: The Evolution of a Short Seller | Frederick Shad Rowe | Talks at Google
description:
Frederick "Shad" Rowe is a long-only consumer focused investor with a stellar track record over 3 decades. In this talk, Shad shares stories from his days as a short seller in the 80s, his model of three stages of a company, the philosophy of better-faster-cheaper, and the art of customer focus.

Moderated by Pranesh Srinivasan.
summary: The video argues that successful large companies often share common traits such as global reach, a massive customer base, and the ability to expand their product offerings. It suggests that companies like Southwest Airlines, Starbucks, Costco, and Amazon have achieved success by evolving through specific stages of growth and operational efficiency. Additionally, the speaker highlights the importance of customer service responses, noting that heroic gestures from companies like Constellation Brands can lead to significant investment profits, whereas standard responses from others like McDonald's are less impactful.

transcript: [MUSIC PLAYING] [APPLAUSE] PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So Shad, I thought maybe we could begin with how you got started on the investing journey? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, my father was in the advertising business for most of his life, and he recommended to me that I buy some Central Airlines with some money I made in the summer on a construction job. So I bought 200 shares of Central Airlines at $2.25 for $450. And I met the Chief Executive Officer, whose name was Lamar Muse. And they came over to my parents' house one time and had dinner. And my mother's dog bit his wife on the nose. [LAUGHTER] They didn't leave, but it went to show you he was a good sport and resilient. So that was something kind of funny. But anyway, the stock went up. It was acquired about a year and a half later by Frontier Airlines for $14 a share. So $2.25 turned into $14 pretty quickly. And I just thought, this beats sitting out in the sun carrying forms around. And I was hooked for life. And that was a good success to start with. I had a lot of failures after that. But I kind of figured it all out eventually. Maybe I have, I don't know. We'll see. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Wow. So did you start investing right away, or-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I bought a little. So I'd hear something, and I'd buy stock, and just hearing something about a stock isn't a very good investment system, because you hear it from people who don't know what they're talking about. It took a while to figure out who did know what they were talking about and who didn't. But I'm always fascinated by it and always interested in it. And you know, I kid around about myself, but my wife took me to this event every year called "Art About Town." And you would bid on paintings, and I would bid on paintings for less than I figured the frame value was. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Less than the frame value? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Less than the frame value, because I was a value investor. And so people would say, well, did you make money doing it? I said, no, I never recognized a penny-- they're all horrible. But at least, I had some cheap frames. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Wow. Shad, I think somewhere in the mid '70s, you also started a banking or a brokerage operation, right? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I worked for this firm called Schneider, Bernet & Hickman. And I was a Syndicate Manager. I would bid the new issues. I would look at the new issues and try to get the firm into the deals. And then I left there, and you know, I wanted to start my own firm, which I called Rowe and Company, Investment Bankers/Brokers. We really were just a brokerage firm and did a little investment banking, but not much. And then I did that and traded for the firm's account and made a little money. And then in 1985, I decided to start a fund to share the joys of short selling, which I was doing a lot of, because the skyline in Dallas was just pure cranes-- like it is here, now. But you know, there were see-through buildings everywhere, and I figured somebody bad was going to happen, so I started short selling. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Were you short selling stocks or real estate? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, stocks-- bank stocks, real estate stocks, real estate-related stocks. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: What was the thesis, there? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: The thesis was it was terribly overbuilt, and everyone was going go broke, which I was absolutely right on. And they did. And so I wouldn't say that was fun, but it was good to be right. In fact, if I'd saved my money and waited until things really broke down, I could have made some great buys. And it just shows how every dark cloud has a silver lining kind of deal. So I could've done-- it's just a matter of which side you're looking at it. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Do you think getting the timing right was important with the short selling? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Of course it was, sure. And you know, you know what I found out was that-- if you buy stock, and it goes down, the most you can lose is the money that you put up. And as it goes down some more, you have a smaller problem, and you don't worry about. But if you short a stock, and it goes up-- you're just sick, you can't even breathe, because you can have unlimited loss potential-- you could die and be incapacitated and lose every dime you have. There's an overpriced stock service I took for a while-- late '80s-- and they recommended shorting Microsoft. And every couple of months, they'd say, hold for a better exit point. Well, hell, they lost all their money. So it's not a good solid business, and when I was doing it, interest rates were high, real rates were high, and broker's call was about where the prime was. So if you put up treasury bills and then shorted stock, you'd get a broker's call on the short position, which would mean that you'd be up 15% when you started, and it was pretty good. And now, of course, you have to pay to borrow them, so you're down when you start, so there's a big difference, there. I didn't figure that out until later, but that's why it was attractive. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Right, and taxes also were-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Oh, taxes were also the same. There were the same taxes on dividends and interest and short sales, and short-swing profits and long-term profits. Everything was taxed the same, so it didn't matter. And so that was another little added factor. Plus, you really never had to cover. You could take the money and pair the trades off, you know what I mean-- cover it versus the box, which would mean you could buy it back-- hold a long position and short position, all at $0.25 a share or something. You'd never have to pay taxes for it. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Could you explain that a little bit, Shad, for us? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Sure. You know, if you're shorting versus the box of stock, you would borrow the shares that you had bought and deliver them against your short position or hold them against your short position. So you would have covered, but not recovered. But everything would be blocked out, and you could just keep the tax money. And then that was outlawed in the Tax Rule of 1985. But that made it a little bit better business then. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So you were getting paid to borrow, the taxes were favorable, and the market was not fairly valued according to that. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: No, and there was a lot more retail investing then than there was the last few years. So not as smart. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So why did you give up short selling? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, it becomes all-consuming. You know, you'd think you'd feel better about it as you get older, but it hurts worse. And my mother, typically, would just always try to be optimistic about things, and one time, she said-- Shaddie, don't worry, I'm sure something terrible will happen. [LAUGHTER] And that didn't make me feel any better, but that was sort of the idea. You know, you were looking for bad outcomes all the time, which, you know, it's a happier life, if you're looking for good outcomes. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: And so after you gave up short selling, you moved on to finding small, local companies in Texas. Can you talk to us a little bit about that? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, actually, in the time between Central Airlines-- I also owned small companies, I owned Southwest Airlines when they had three and then four airplanes-- so I knew something about the airline business, and I knew something about advertising business a little bit, because of my father. And so I was sort of set up-- I owned some things on those lines. And I find that one kind of door leads to another, and everything is kind of connected. We're all connected. And so, between my father-- and you know, who I'm much more friendly toward now than I was when he was alive, unfortunately-- but you could kind of get a feel for different businesses. So in the end, the shorts would eventually turned into longs. I bought back-- I owned-- it was short-- WPP Group in 1991, and then covered in '92 and covered in '91 and then ended up buying it and made a lot on it. And Southwest Airlines, I did very well on. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So when did you buy your first shares of Southwest Airlines? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: About 1974. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: 1974? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: That's about-- I still have some. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: You still have the same shares-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: No, no, not the same shares. I sold most of it, but the stuff is very valuable. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Wow. Would you know how much the revenues have compounded by or the stock price has compounded by since you bought it? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Oh, it was probably 27%. It was huge. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: 20% over 30+ years. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yes. It's amazing what it did. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: What was it about how Southwest that got your attention? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, Lamar Muse. He's the same guy that was the head of Central Airlines. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Right. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: And so I felt like I knew him. And it was obvious to me that they were doing something better, faster, cheaper. They were flying between Dallas and San Antonio and Houston on a tight schedule and doing it for not much than the price of a bus ticket. So the traffic was expanding. They were stimulating the market, and it was growing. And they did that everywhere they went all over the United States. And now, they've gone abroad. And you know, it's a better story. They have one airplane that they fly. They just threw an engine out, I saw. It was on the news, today. But it was just a once in a lifetime kind of deal. And to do it in an airline is very unusual, because really it never has shown loss in all these years. And other ones went broke all the time. But they didn't put their customers first. They put themselves first. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: And their employees, too. They treat-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah, they treat everybody well. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: --very well, yeah. So around 15 years ago, maybe, or a little older than that, you changed your outlook again-- focusing on companies that can scale-- do things faster, better, cheaper for the customers. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: How did this change happen, and maybe, give us some examples? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, it was part of an odd man out kind of thing. You know, if you own stock in a company, you're kind of second rate compared to the management. You know, they don't always tell you the truth, and they're manipulating you. But if you think the company is really doing something for the stakeholders, for the shareholders, for the customers than for themselves, you feel a lot better about it. So I feel better as an investor if I've invested in a company like that. So better, faster, cheaper, and for-- and not to-- the customer, and to the delight of the customer. And be on a scale that if it works in-- oh, and another thing in advertising, I did-- this WPP Group I talked to you about, where Martin Sorrell just left, he got fired. But he said that the word globalization is a misnomer, that the better word is Americanization. People all over the world really want to live the way we do, here. I don't know whether you believe that. I think there's something to it. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Yeah. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: So if it's a success here, it can be a success elsewhere. And that's certainly been the case of airlines and of Starbucks, Amazon-- you know, all these companies operate throughout the world. And you know, you used to talk about the law of large numbers. Well, hell, you need to own a stock that has a large number, because there are a large number of people in the world and a large number of square miles to cover, and you've got to get out there before someone beats you to it. I think these big companies have a huge advantage, now. Rather than big, cumbersome oafs, like they used to be, they're really big and strong and powerful, and they just win-win-win. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So following up on that, Shad, recently I think you wrote about the necessity of large numbers-- that large numbers are not just needed to compete, but to actually succeed. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Right. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So can you talk to us a little bit about that? Why do you think large numbers are a necessity? And maybe give us an example of a company that you think has efficiency going for it? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: We can't talk about Google, can we? PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Uh. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I'm teasing. Well, all of them, really. You know, Southwest Airlines now is going to Mexico. They're going in the Caribbean. They're big enough to do it, and no one would sit aside and let Southwest do to them what they did. I mean, Southwest, I think couldn't happen again, because people are just smarter. I think that board compositions have changed. I think the people are more attentive. And you know, the kind of dull, kind of half senile Chief Executive Officer who sits there and acts like a dictator-- they're over. And women on the boards have helped, I think. And there is just more visibility, and it's hard to be as secretive as people used to be. I think that governance is better, and I think the opportunities are better perceived. And investors aren't any smarter, but I think the whole investment situation has improved. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: And I think you also stressed on efficiency, right, Shad? And you say that Costco is not just efficient, but elegant. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Oh yeah, it's great. It's fun to be there, fun to shop there. You save money. You get great products, you get great value. You see the same people there. And I think the shopping is sort of an adventure. It's kind of fun. And they put things in the store just to get you back. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: How did you approach Costco as an investment decision? Did you-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I liked going there. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: OK. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: It's probably as simple as that. I thought, if I like it, other people probably like it, and they do. You want to save money, you want to get value-- you don't care about the brand name. I mean, the brand-- what is it, Kingwood, is it? It's great stuff. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: The Kirkland? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Kirkland. Well, I'm losing my mind, here, but yeah. It's really good. I like everything about it. One time, I was at this investment group, and the deal on the dinner we were going to was that the person who had the worst bottle of wine had to buy dinner. And so I went, and I took a bottle of wine that my wife had picked out from Constellation Brands. I can't remember the name of it, but it was a 92 on the wine or whatever board, or something. But anyway, I heard the waitress complaining and saying, this wine is flawed, the cork is no good. And then they didn't put wrap it up in tin foil, so I know what it is. I said, all right, I give up-- it's me, I'll buy dinner. And I wrote a letter to Jim Sinegal, saying that I'd had this horrible experience. And by golly, Constellation Brands sent me a gift certificate for Costco to give me my money back. You know, I just made a huge profit on it and bought more stock. And then I did the same thing to McDonald's and talked about something terrible that happened there. And I got a form letter back-- sorry for your bad experience and just nothing. But you know, that's sort of a heroic response-- just going overboard, bending over backwards to make people happy. And if the customer comes first, you get ahead. And if it doesn't, you get behind. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So I think when you said-- customer comes first, I'm reminded of another one of your nice characterizations about stage one companies, stage two companies, and stage three companies. And these aren't to do with size of the company or age of the company. They're with how the company-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: How they act. In stage one-- everything's new-- you're doing something better, faster, cheaper for the customer. Your stock is soaring. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Can you give us examples of each stage? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, any little company that takes off. Southwest Airlines has been kind of stage one the whole career it's had. And stage two is maybe like a Starbucks, where they start selling tea and different food and trying to get more money from the same person. And stage three is most airlines and banks and everything else, where there's no question they're out to get you. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So how do you detect this change between stage two and stage three, Shad? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I'm a customer, just like you are. It's obvious, isn't it? That's what I think. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So what are the hallmarks, Shad, of a great business? Like, these stage two, stage one kind of business-- what are the hallmarks? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I would love to find a business that was doing something better, faster, cheaper on a scale that could be taken globally, that I'd seen it work in the United States, that had great management. You know, I don't know how you define that, but you know it when you see it. And some valuation that somehow you could think was reasonable. And that sounded like that-- I was laughing the other day about that David Allan Coe song. You know, what was it-- I think your song is perfect, but you haven't said anything about mama or trains or being drunk or falling off the bus-- but all the ingredients are there, just like the ingredients are there for a perfect stock. And you're always looking for the perfect stock. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Do you do you focus on capital intensivity at all, when you look at a great company? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Capital intensiv-- capital what? PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Capital intensiveness-- how they use their balance sheet. Are those things you look at? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I look at it. But I presume they know more than I do, so I'm not too judgmental about it. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: OK. So let's invert that a little bit. You know, like Carl Jacobi and Charlie Munger. So what are some things you want to avoid in a business? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, If you were still short, I'd want the same thing. You know, if it's not doing better, faster, cheaper, it's doing something worse. It irritates people. They don't like it, and business is going down. And it has no potential overseas, because it has no potential in the United States. You'd invert it, and it would be perfect inversion. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Are there industries or sectors that you would avoid? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I don't think that way. I think of the ones that I would be attracted to. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: OK. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: And clearly, technology is an area-- home building is kind of interesting, because all the Millennials are living at home, and their parents are getting tired of them. And I think they'll buy houses at some point. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Technology and home building are sectors-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah, kind of the whole modern home, you know, the smart home. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Right. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: So I know this guy that runs a [? Pull-T-- ?] PRANESH SRINIVASAN: [? Pull-T ?] group, yes. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah, and then I don't think it matters too much, but they're all going to have it, when the technology finally brought in house to-- bring the house into the modern age. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: If it can continue on another Charlie Munger-ism-- we learn more from our mistakes than our successes. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I oughta know a lot, then. [LAUGHTER] PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So after short selling, you know, once you moved to being a long and being a consumer focused investor, what are one or two mistakes you've made that you want to talk about? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: One of those, I don't want to talk about. And the smaller companies-- there was a company in Dallas called Employers Casualty Insurance Company that did workers compensation. And it was a cheap, cheap stock. And it had always been a great company and had a great balance sheet. And the management wouldn't talk to me. And I presumed that meant that it was so good, they didn't want to share the information. And so I bought it. And they wouldn't return the phone call, and it went broke. That's a bad example, or a good example of that. Another one-- you know, I had some success with Southwest Airlines several times. And I got very interested in Greyhound buses. And even my wife said, what are you thinking about-- no one rides a bus. And you couldn't see that no one was on the buses, because the windows were tinted. So that was a painful one. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So you probably picked up a lot of trading techniques as a short seller, looking at price, volume, maybe margin calls, technicals. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: No. I didn't learn anything. [LAUGHTER] PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So do you look at anything other than the customer experience and fundamentals when you invest in a business? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, it's nice if the stock is off for the wrong reason. That's always a good one. They're panicked about something-- the shareholders are panicked over something they shouldn't be panicked over. That's a good reason to do it. You get a better bargain that way. But I think in the long term, it doesn't make that much difference when you buy it, if you buy the right company. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So let's focus on that a little bit-- the valuation, right. How do you approach valuation when deciding to buy a business? What is an upper bound you're willing to pay? How do you arrive at that? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I'd just want to see how you can pay 10 times what you thought it was eventually going to earn. That would be OK with me, if you had a pretty high degree of confidence in it. Because with interest rates where they are, you've got to think what you can do with your money. And if people say, well, the market is very overpriced, and the NASDAQ sells at 33 times earnings or whatever it sells at-- well, you know, what's the yield on a 10-year government? 3%-- that's 33 times earnings. And that's the most they're going to earn. So the companies have a chance to earn a lot more. So I think stocks are probably cheap relative to your choices of what you can do with the money. Real estate isn't any better. Farming-- well, I don't know what you're going to do. But your choices are limited. You know, stock is people, it's real estate, it's capital, it's machines. It's being put together by smart people, working and creating value and growing-- pretty exciting. And it doesn't excite people very much, now, but it will. They haven't thought it through. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So once you buy a stock, ideally, Shad, you never want to sell it. You write fairly well that selling creates two problems, right? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Right. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: The tax problem, and the problem when-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Then you pay taxes, and you've got to replace the investment. You've got to be right twice. All you've got to do on a real growth cycle is to be right once. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: But sometimes you still have to sell, Shad. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Sure. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: And do you sell because the situation changes, or do you sell also sometimes because the price runs up too much? How do you think of it? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I've done a little bit of that. You know, this WPP Group, which I bought years ago-- I sold some in 2000. It was selling at a crazy price, and didn't get it all sold, but I kept it. And then you know I knew Martin Sorrell and watched him. But then I watched other companies come along, like this one. And you know, it was hurting their business very badly. So I eventually sold it. And I made good sales, too. That would be a reason-- you know, if the business is fundamentally changed by technology or by something that they haven't done. That would be the reason to sell it, or the management's bad, or something had changed that you could see. But not because it didn't show relative strength or something crazy like that. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Shad, if we can shift gears a little bit, you've spoken about the need for pension funds to be simple in their investing process. And recently, there have been incidents of funds that have invested in exotic foreign agriculture and things that didn't work out well. Why do you think this happens, and what can be done to improve this? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: If you'll think of yourself as a stock, I think it helps. You know, you have more money coming in than going out, hopefully, and you all are in there to buy stocks, and your estate grows. And you get a better job or you don't get a better job, but you're spending less than you're saving, then you're grow up and you're going to be rich old guy or girl or whatever. And that's the way it works. And these pension funds have more money going out than coming in. And compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world, but when it's working against you, you can't beat it. That's what's happening in these pension funds-- they promise more than they can deliver. And so they're saying they're making money-- or they're only 75% funded, or something like that. But really, they're going to go broke. And you can be an alarmist about it. I got fired-- I was the Chairman of the Texas Review Board for 12 years or something. And you know, Governor Perry finally fired me. He got tired of listening, tired of hearing me. But compound interest is a wonderful thing to have on your side and a terrible thing to have working against you. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Do you think that's likely to change in the coming years, the way-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Oh, sure, it'll change-- like, the sun will come up in the west or the east or wherever it does. You know, no. They're immutable laws. It isn't going to change. Behavior isn't going to change. People get hold of other people's money. They like it. It gives them power, and they want to be smart. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So Shad, one of the books, I think, that have really influenced you has been "Money Masters," by John Train. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: What about the book influenced you? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, he's a good money manager. And he understood the distinctions that investors were making in their minds. It's just a good survey. And nothing's changed since then. No one had ever studied investment managers before. They were just kind of like clerks, or something. Then they became kind of larger than life, sometimes, and it became interesting to people. But the thing I found interesting-- he's very thoughtful, and one time I said, after studying all these people-- value investors and all this-- how did you become a growth stock manager, at, like, T. Rowe Price? And he said that value investors are really kind of glorified accountants. They're looking at the gap between their perceived value and what the assets are going to be worth and its market capitalization and trying to close the difference. And then when they do it, they've got to go buy something else. So it's a constant turnover process. If you ever make a mistake, you pay a lot of taxes, and you've lost all your money. But a growth stock investor, which, he said-- that suited his nature-- you're really kind of a futurologist-- looking in the future and trying to figure out what's going to happen. He said that suited his nature, so that's what he did. That makes perfect sense to me. And it requires fewer people, and you just have to be right a couple of times in your life. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: When we were speaking earlier with one of your colleagues, [INAUDIBLE],, you spoke about the spectrum of investors-- short sellers, activists, long only investors. Do you want to share that with us? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I was just saying that short sellers really think that they're the smartest people on Earth, that they're much smarter than these managements. And they're so smart, they'll risk their whole stash to prove they're right. And they either go broke or have nervous breakdowns or just shoot themselves. I mean, I know a guy who tried to just killed himself. But it's a terrible life. And then the next ones are the activist investors-- activists. They think they're smarter than management, too. They're going to tell them how to do it. So they just get in there and start saying, do this, do this, do that. And we want to sell the company and want to make these fees. And then-- PRANESH SRINIVASAN: The value investors. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: And then the value investors I've already talked about. You can rank them all. And then the growth stock investors just think-- this company is smarter than I am, they know the business better than I do, plus it's a great business. And it if isn't, I'll get out of it. That's how you have a slight advantage, there. You want to put yourself on the side where you have an advantage, and they don't. So if you perceive that there's a long term future for the business-- they're doing simply better, faster, cheaper and for the customer, you can buy it at a reasonable price, and if you're wrong, you can sell it-- that's a pretty good deal. And that's one I think I want to take. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So Shad, I want to get a little personal with this question for you. So around two decades ago, you were diagnosed with Parkinson's. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Shortly afterwards you considered shutting down your fund. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: But then you chose not to shut it down. Maybe you should walk us through that. And also, after that, you've stated that having Parkinson's has actually made you a better person. Can you talk to us-- why you feel that? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, Michael J. Fox, I'm on his board. He calls up-- Parkinson's is a gift that keeps on taking. But I think it makes you a little humble and more appreciative of what you did have going right. You have to make adjustments to it. But my first reaction was what the hell is going on here? And I thought, well, I'll do everybody a favor and shut the fund down. And I gave all the money back. I had some stocks that were hard to get out of-- they were illiquid. And so I dragged my feet and then decided-- what else am I going to do? So I changed my mind and have had a good record ever since. I had a good record the whole time, but yeah, it changes your life a little bit. And you appreciate the things that go your way, and the things that don't, you don't worry as much about, which is meaning to say-- I'm kind of a completely pleasant personality-- is not. But you know, I think investing is a matter of finding out who you are and where you fit in the world and how it all fits together. You know, I don't know whose saying it is, but-- if you don't know who you are, the stock market is an expensive place to find out-- is true. But if you fit your nature with your investment style, and it makes economic sense, you can probably do pretty well. If you think of yourself as a stock-- where you have more coming in than going out-- and so you're doing something with the money-- in other words, you're managing your cash flow-- you're going to end up being a rich old guy or girl or whatever. And that makes sense to me. So I feel like the game is going my way. And I feel like that's the way anybody who thought about it should go. And if you listen to the television-- the stocks are under accumulation, it's breaking out, it's breaking down, it's lacking support-- I'm selling, I'm selling, buy-sell, buy-sell. Just pay a lot of commissions and dealer spreads and lose your money and talk more. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: So Shad, before we open it up to the audience for questions, I want to ask you one question that we ask all our guests. What is some advice you would give the personal investor, someone who's starting their journey today, maybe investing their first few dollars and trying to make compounding work for them? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I'd say the same thing-- who are you, what do you like? You know, are you a cheerleader, or are you a booer? Do you know you want the home team to win, or do you want the home team to lose? And pick companies you like-- you like the management, you think they have a bright future, you like dealing with them, you think they're good people, and just sit on it and own it. And think of yourself as a partial owner of a business, just like you're the owner of your entire business, which is your life. So that's kind of Warren Buffett 101, combined with a little pop psychology and my experience. And that's what I would do. That's what I'm trying to do. Does that makes sense? PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Yeah. No, thank you, Shad. Thank you so much for that. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Fun being here. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: I think we'll open it up to audience questions. And I have a few more in case we have time at the end of audience questions. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: All right, yeah. AUDIENCE: Thank you for your talk. That's very inspiring. So I have a question about the large number as a necessity. I was wondering if you think there is the risk of the anti-trust once the company goes large, and the large member goes-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Sure. That's a terrifying aspect of it. But usually the litigation starts coming when they're trying to use the government to protect themselves from competition or something. So I don't know. It'll be interesting. I watched another company the other day, talking on the television about its issues and problems. But I think that these congressmen and these state legislators, they're so busy that they don't have time to understand anything very clearly. And you know, if the business is still good, and will probably survive and do fine. And they have constituencies that-- people vote, and so I don't worry about it too much. I'm worried about it some, but not too much. I think it's overrated. Does that makes sense? That answers your question? AUDIENCE: Yeah, it makes sense. Thanks. AUDIENCE: You talked about better, faster, cheaper. What is one business that's better, faster, cheaper that you would like to own, but you don't because of price or whatever other reason? And I have a second part question. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I don't have any of those. I bought them. [LAUGHTER] AUDIENCE: What is something that you owned in the past that is no longer, better, faster, cheaper, and why? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, let's see-- McDonald's. And you know, they're getting beaten by lots of people, now. And PetSmart, which has started selling very expensive products. You save money-- put your dog up at the warehouse stores, and put them down and add more functions in them. But it was not as good a company-- what they could do to the dog or do to you or how they could trick you. But really, I'm just trying to find the ones that are good and hold them. I sold WPP, which-- I don't know, what I made, 33 times on my money-- and the reason was the competitors, online competitors were doing it better, faster, cheaper, and getting more for the money. And you watch regular television, now, and the ads on it for drugs that-- you know, the side effects might be that you'll die, crying for your mother. They're just terrible, off-putting. And so, an ad that applies to you directly-- that you and you only see-- that's structured, that will tell you something that you want to hear seems like a better deal to me. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: I think you had also written about CarMax, which, back in the day, was excellent pricing, right? But with discoverability, now-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah, the advantage is gone, because everybody knows what everybody paid for everything. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: Because of internet and Kelley Blue Book. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Sure. AUDIENCE: One last question. We had Mr. Schwab visit us, I think, about two years ago, from Charles Schwab. And he talked about how, in his words-- Charles Schwab continues to deliver their services to their customers better, faster, cheaper. How do you think about Charles Schwab, say, compared to, say T. Rowe, which you do on? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Compared to T. Rowe? PRANESH SRINIVASAN: T. Rowe, yeah. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I got a good price on T. Rowe. I'm really to get out of it. AUDIENCE: Do you think Charles Schwab does better, faster, cheaper? You are in that industry, so probably you know better about who does? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, I think that right now T. Rowe Price probably does better, because they're focused on growth companies. And the market isn't paying the premium that its certainly capable of paying for those companies. I can remember-- I was not in the market at that time, but-- the Nifty 50 were induplicable companies that would always be in people's portfolios, regardless, and had always grown to-- they all sold at 100 times earnings, 1973. So I think that sort of thing can happen again-- maybe have a World 50, World Nifty 50. You know, you talk about Bitcoin-- well, hell, Coca Cola stock used to be like Bitcoin. Or the technology companies are like that. I think that could easily happen. And I think that these companies can make the-- you know, they know more about their businesses than I do, and they can buy them for stock or buy them for cash, and everybody turns into a Warren Buffett, kind of. I mean, what did we learn from Warren Buffett. I mean, he started out with, you know, delivering papers and turned that into becoming the richest guy in the world for a while. And what did he do-- he just had an obsession with money and never spent it, and just compounded, compounded, compounded. AUDIENCE: I always wonder about nonprofit investments. And when I think of Buffett or Gates and a lot of philanthropic investments, you know-- is it in the context of philanthropy versus giving away. What's this actual investment and being able to manage it? And I always wondered what the thought process is when the rich decide to go one way or the other. And I'm just curious to hear your thoughts. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: On accumulating money? AUDIENCE: Philanthropy, or you know, investment in change in the context of larger good-- how do investors think about it? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I think about it all the time. And I don't-- I'm usually disappointed by what I discover about what was really happening. I mean, you know people get old, and they want to have hospitals named after them, and they want to invest in health care. And the health care people are just charging more every year. And it's become too big a burden. Not to complain about it, but yeah, I think it's an issue. You know, you don't want to die with all your money. And you'd rather have you decide what to do with it than let someone else decide what to do with it. Certainly. any one is going to do better than the government, probably. But I think it's a big issue. We don't live forever, because we all think we will. Yes, ma'am. AUDIENCE: Hi. I wonder what's your advice about risk controlling for personal investors who don't have much time to investigate what's going on in the market. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, you'd beat 90% of the investors, if you just bought the S&P 500 index from Vanguard or Fidelity or something like that. That's what most people ought to do, then they wouldn't worry about what the individual stocks are. You know, you put 90% of your money in those index funds and then play with other money, just like your play money and have fun with it. I mean-- my advice. AUDIENCE: I really enjoy your sort of three stage model on how companies sort of get fat and then get lazy and then, you know, get eaten. One question I have is how frequently do companies that you've purchased turn into a different stage? Or obviously, you're trying to buy ones that always stay in stage one. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: That's very hard to do. AUDIENCE: --worse case-- end up in stage two, but-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Because they're successful in stage one, and that leads to problems. Just like with people. It's just exactly like a person. And you know, at some point, the company is successful, and it wants to do something else. And the individual wants to do something else that didn't make them the money in the first place. And this is exactly the same thing. So you want to make enough money so that your comfortable and you get your needs taken care of, but that's enough, probably, unless it becomes a game or an obsession. But you're right, exactly. It is the same thing as with a person. AUDIENCE: Can I ask you a brief follow-up, which is-- in a profile of you from 2016, you mention that you aim to have about 15 stocks in your portfolio at any given time, and you sort of sell off the worst performing one every year and try to replace it. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Yeah. AUDIENCE: And that incidentally you also mention that by concentration, only about six of them make up about 70% of the actual portfolio by value. Is that a fairly constant sort of performance metric? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, it just is what happens. This is what happened to me. But I'd like to-- I'm probably at about 12 or 13 stocks, at most. And most of the money is in very few stocks. But you want to be diversified to the point that you've got the odds in your favor, but not to the point that you don't keep up with them. And I'm being a little bit more disciplined about it than I used to be, but it's hard to sell a stock once you have a profit in it. It's hard to sell it, pay the taxes, make up the net worth, and pay the dealer spread and make the money back. So what you tend to do is own some other companies at low cost. But you know, if you want to step out, you've got to sell them. And they've got to fit what you really think is happening. I mean, I was saying the same thing 10 years ago, but my portfolio has completely turned over since then. And the reason is I have better companies now, I think-- knock wood. AUDIENCE: As companies grow, the culture is very difficult to maintain, right? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: What is? AUDIENCE: Especially when bureaucracy creeps in. What made you believe that Southwest will continue keeping its culture in the future? FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Its culture? AUDIENCE: Yes. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Well, they've got a good guy-- Gary Kelly, who's running it. They've always had good Chief Executive Officers. But it's hard to change a culture for the worse, and it's hard to change for the better. And you know, I like to pick on American Airlines, but it just seems like they invariably do the exact thing that I don't want them to do-- like, changing a reservation. Southwest, they let you change your time. American Airlines-- you have to buy another ticket. By the time they tag their penalties and everything else on you, it was stupid. I don't understand it. And so who is your fidelity owed to? It's owed to your customer and to the shareholders. You know, you've got stakeholders in any business, and you've got to treat them right. And a lot of times these professional managements get hold of these companies, and they think they're the ones to be served-- they need to serve themselves first. And everybody can see that, and they react against it. And they don't share in the business and they go on, which is fine, I guess. It makes plenty of money. But it could have made more and had more fun and contributed to society, rather than not. AUDIENCE: If I may ask another question-- I understand that for a short seller, it's hard also because you not only need to get your decisions right, you also need to get your timing right. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Right. AUDIENCE: As a value investor, you know, I guess you're not supposed to time the market. And we know, it's very hard. But I keep wondering, because for example, as of right now, we are in, like, a late part of the cycle. I wonder, being understanding and we should not timing the market-- one, if there is a strategy you think you master would deal slightly differently than the beginning of the cycle? I don't know-- it's kind of a-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: I'm glad to know that we're at the end of the cycle. I found that our from you. I don't know that we are at all. I don't have any idea. I think that from the time I've been in the business, the general public's attitude is much less interested in the stock market. And there are fewer shares or fewer companies that are public. There are better companies, now-- they're better run. And it's just as competitive, and they make more money. The profitability is higher. I think stocks are a heck of a deal relative to what else you can do with your money. And if you get a few of those other things right-- you know, the better, faster, cheaper and for the customer and to the delight of the customer, and if it works in the United States and can be taken internationally-- I don't see how you miss. And when you find out, I hope you'll call me and tell me about it. PRANESH SRINIVASAN: All right. I think we are out of time. Thank you so much, Shad, for-- FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Is that OK? PRANESH SRINIVASAN: --coming and speaking with us. I think we should all-- really enjoyed it. [APPLAUSE]
